\textbf{Source.} Tadelis (2013), \emph{Game Theory: An Introduction}, Exercise 4.10 ``Popsicle Stands'', p.~78 {[}PDF 97{]}. Reproduced verbatim. Answer in the source: none in the book (the preface, p.~xiii, says about half are solved on Princeton UP's website; not checked).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Popsicle Stands:} Five lifeguard towers are lined up along a beach; the leftmost tower is number 1 and the rightmost tower is number 5. Two vendors, players 1 and 2, each have a popsicle stand that can be located next to one of five towers. There are 25 people located next to each tower, and each person will purchase a popsicle from the stand that is closest to him or her. That is, if player 1 locates his stand at tower 2 and player 2 at tower 3, then 50 people (at towers 1 and 2) will purchase from player 1, while 75 (from towers 3, 4, and 5) will purchase from vendor 2. Each purchase yields a profit of \$1.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  Specify the strategy set for each player. Are there any strictly dominated strategies?
\item
  Find the set of strategies that survive rationalizability.
\end{enumerate}
\end{quote}
